title: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
chapter: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
goal: Worked example: any four whole numbers contain two whose difference is a multiple of 3.

scenes.visual: Four blank cards. Claim text: "Any four different whole numbers include two whose difference is a multiple of 3." Question: "Why must this be true?"
scenes.narration: Here is a claim to prove. Choose any four different whole numbers. Two of them will always have a difference that is a multiple of three. Why must that be true?

scenes.visual: Three boxes labelled 0, 1, 2. Text: "remainder on division by 3".
scenes.narration: When any whole number is divided by three, the remainder is zero, one or two. Use those three remainders as three boxes.

scenes.visual: Four cards drop towards three boxes; one box receives two cards.
scenes.narration: Four numbers go into three boxes, so at least two numbers land in the same box. They have the same remainder.

scenes.visual: Two numbers written as "3a + r" and "3b + r". Subtracting: the r's cancel, leaving 3(a - b).
scenes.narration: Write those two numbers as three a plus r and three b plus r. When you subtract, the remainders cancel, leaving three times a minus b. That is a multiple of three.

scenes.visual: Example cards 2, 6, 10, 13 sort into boxes: 6 in box 0; 10 and 13 in box 1; 2 in box 2. Then cards 1, 2, 3 shown as a set of three with all different boxes.
scenes.narration: Test it. Take two, six, ten and thirteen. Ten and thirteen both have remainder one, and their difference is three. Could three numbers be enough? No: one, two and three all have different remainders, and no difference is a multiple of three. So four is the smallest number that guarantees it.

scenes.visual: Line: "same remainder gives a difference that is a multiple". Notebook prompt.
scenes.narration: The boxes proved the claim for every choice at once. Rebuild the proof, then answer this: how many whole numbers must you choose to be sure that two of them differ by a multiple of ten?

notebook_exercise: How many whole numbers guarantee two that differ by a multiple of 10?
notebook_answer: 11, since there are 10 possible last digits.
